function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

{"content": "     1|Tomorrow Is Still Open
     2|
     3|A Memoir by Bob Mills
     4|
     5|# Part One: The Ignition
     6|
     7|## Chapter One: The Shock
     8|
     9|### Summer 1958, Northern Michigan
    10|
    11|The summer of 1958 smelled like pine sap and lake water, like cedar shingles baking in the heat and the faint mothball ghost of a cabin closed up too long. I was six years old, and that summer marks the precise moment my memory clicks on. Everything before it is fog and family story. Everything after is mine.
    12|
    13|We'd driven up from lower Michigan, my father at the wheel, my mother navigating with quiet competence. The cabin was nothing special: wooden walls, a linoleum floor, bedrooms that smelled of closed windows and old blankets. But to a six-year-old, it was an undiscovered continent. Every drawer held a mystery. Every cupboard concealed a treasure.
    14|
    15|That afternoon, the adults drifted to the front room. Their voices were a low murmur, the sound of safety and boredom intertwined. I was alone in the kitchen, and that kitchen had become my laboratory.
    16|
    17|My father's car keys lay on the counter. Ordinary keys—the kind any man carried in 1958—but they wore a puzzle fob that seemed to me a piece of art. A small wooden carving, Native American in design, interlocking geometric pieces fitted together with a precision that demanded investigation. I picked up the keys. The metal was cool against my palm. I turned the fob over and over, tracing the carved ridges where a craftsman's tool had met the wood.
    18|
    19|But childhood curiosity is a hungry animal. It cannot be satisfied long by one mystery when another waits nearby.
    20|
    21|As I twisted the fob in my small fingers, my eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.
    22|
    23|I knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." My mother had said it. My father had said it. It was a rule as fixed as not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in my hand. Those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.
    24|
    25|*What would happen?*
    26|
    27|---
    28|
    29|I remember gripping the key shaft. I remember my hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. I remember the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.
    30|
    31|The key made contact.
    32|
    33|Electricity is invisible. We see its fingerprints—light, heat, motion—but the current itself hides behind walls, a ghost we've domesticated. In that moment, I met that ghost directly. The shock surged through my body with the indifferent authority of physics acting on matter. My muscles clenched. My arm locked. The force threw me backward across the kitchen. I landed in a heap against the far wall.
    34|
    35|Darkness. Not the gentle dark of sleep, but a violent absence—a blink of the universe. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped thing. My hand—*oh, my hand*—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration, the echo of the current that had passed through it. Time became elastic. Those moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours. I sat on that linoleum floor, dazed, my body having learned something that all the warnings in the world could never teach.
    36|
    37|Then came the footsteps. Hurried. Panicked. My parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed—my mother's eyes wide, my father's jaw set. They found me crumpled against the wall, the keys on the floor between me and the outlet, the story written clearly without a single word spoken.
    38|
    39|The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment dressed in fear, delivered in tones that betrayed how close they had come to something worse. I was told what I already knew, what my body had just learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight.
    40|
    41|And yet.
    42|
    43|Here is the part that still surprises me, seventy years later. Despite the terror. Despite the scolding. Despite the tingle that lingered in my hand for hours afterward—I felt exhilaration. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, I had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. I had asked a question of the universe—*what will happen?*—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve.
    44|
    45|This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment a child realizes the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.
    46|
    47|### What I Remember vs. What I Was Told
    48|
    49|But here we must pause, because I cannot be entirely certain this memory belongs to me. The mind is a trickster, a master forger of its own past. Cognitive science has proven this beyond doubt: every time we recall a memory, we reconstruct it. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what happened and what we believe happened becomes porous, eventually indistinguishable.
    50|
    51|My mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as I grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—my fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of my body hitting the wall, the expression on my father's face. Did I remember these things? Or did I remember *her* remembering them?
    52|
    53|The memory I carry feels real. I can feel the cool metal of the key. I can taste the ozone in the air afterward. But feeling real and *being* real are different things. A false memory can be as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience. I have studied the neuroscience since then. I know about synaptic plasticity, about long-term potentiation. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. I still cannot say with certainty whether I remember the shock itself or only remember my mother telling me about it.
    54|
    55|Perhaps that ambiguity is itself the lesson.
    56|
    57|### The Spark That Lit a Life
    58|
    59|What is *not* ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of my life. Whether I actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed I had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in me—a fascination with electricity that evolved into a passion for science and technology spanning seven decades.
    60|
    61|In the months and years that followed, I devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. I conducted home experiments—some dangerous, all illuminating. I built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles governing the invisible force that had once thrown me across a kitchen. My parents, recognizing that my curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured my endeavors. They bought me books. They tolerated the mess. They learned to check the fuse box after I had been "working" in the basement.
    62|
    63|That passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars.
    64|
    65|The gift of that moment was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. It taught me that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands we touch the very things we're warned against. It taught me that the most formative moments of our lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether I actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that I *believe* I did—that this belief shaped my curiosity, my career, my very identity.
    66|
    67|The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming.
    68|
    69|That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement. Because something far more distant than a kitchen outlet was about to begin beeping its way across the night sky, and the child who had touched invisible forces in a Michigan cabin was about to discover that the universe held reaches extending far beyond anything he could yet imagine.
    70|
    71|## Chapter 2: The Echoes of Sputnik and a Family Legacy
    72|
    73|The beep came from everywhere and nowhere at once in 1957. Five-year-old Robert Mills sat cross-legged on the worn linoleum floor of his grandparents' living room, his eyes fixed on the radio console that dominated the corner like a mahogany cathedral. The voice on the broadcast spoke words he couldn't fully comprehend—something about Russians, about a silver sphere now circling the Earth, about a new age dawning while America slept. Beep. Beep. Beep. That sound—mechanical, relentless, somehow both cold and alive—would echo through Bob's future memory for the next seven decades. Psychologists have a term for such moments: "flashbulb memories," vivid recollections encoded during times of intense emotion or historical significance. For Bob's generation, Sputnik became exactly that—a neural snapshot burned into the hippocampus, indelible as a brand. He didn't understand then what he was witnessing. How could he? He was five a child of the Midwest, raised in a world where televisions were still novelties and telephones came with party lines. The Space Age might as well have been the Stone Age for all the context his four-year-old mind could provide. Yet something in the following years about the beeping signal registered deep in his subconscious—a recognition that the world had shifted on its axis, that the comfortable boundaries of his young life had suddenly expanded to include not just his street, his town, his country, but the infinite black canvas above.
    74|
    75|### The Builder's Blood
    76|
    77|If Sputnik represented humanity reaching upward, Bob's family roots ran deep into the earth—specifically, into iron rails and coal smoke and the rhythmic chug of locomotive engines. His grandfather was a locomotive engineer, back when that title meant something almost sacred. In the early days of the twentieth century, engineers weren't mere operators; they were craftsmen, masters of machines built by hand in foundries where every piston and valve bore the fingerprints its engineer. A photograph from that era survives in the family archive: young Bob perched atop an enormous black locomotive, his small hand gripping the cast-iron railing, his grandfather standing beside him with a wave that seems to say, *This is yours, boy. This tradition of building, of understanding how things work, of making the immovable move—this is your inheritance.* Bob has no memory of that photograph being taken. What he remembers is the photograph itself— until its edges softened and its colors faded. This is how memory works, he would later understand: not a faithful recording but a palimpsest, written and rewritten, until the original event becomes inseparable from its retellings. His great-grandfather, Robert Charters, carried the storytelling tradition forward with tales that blurred the line between history and legend. When Bob was eight, the old man—already ravaged by consumption, eating only baby food from glass jars that seemed to mock his diminished state—would summon his great-grandson with a gesture learned in another century.  "Remember, lad," he would rasp, his voice carrying the weight of Scottish highlands and Canadian wilderness and the Michigan lumber camps where the Mills family had finally put down roots, "we Mills have the blood of builders and engineers."
    78|
    79|The stories were extraordinary. Knights Templar, his great-grandfather claimed—medieval warrior-monks who had fought bloody battles during the Crusades, then transformed themselves into Europe's master builders, constructing the soaring Gothic cathedrals that still inspired awe. From protectors of pilgrims to moneylenders, from stone masons to bankers—the trajectory seemed both improbable and somehow fitting for a family that would eventually produce locomotive engineers and, in Bob's case, far beyond. Years later, genealogical research would find no documentary evidence of Templar connections. The stories, it seemed, were exactly that—stories, embroidered and enhanced through generations of retelling until they achieved the density of myth. But Bob came to understand that factual accuracy mattered less than the *function* of such tales. They were identity scripts, passed down to give shape to lives that might otherwise feel random and unmoored. Whether his veins actually carried Templar blood was irrelevant; what mattered was that he believed himself part of a lineage of builders, of problem-solvers, of men who looked at raw materials and saw possibility. This, too, was memory at work—not the dry retention of facts, but the active construction of self.
    80|
    81|### The Navy Way
    82|
    83|To understand Bob's father, you must first understand the crucible that forged him. Bob Sr. grew up an only child in a world bounded by the elementary school across the street and the small universe of his family home. When World War II erupted, it pulled him into a vaster and more terrifying reality. At seventeen, he enlisted in the Navy and found himself responsible for the electrical systems of a scow—a flat-bottomed workhorse of a vessel that served the fleet in dangerous unsung and essential ways. The Navy of that era was not the modern, technologically sophisticated force we know today. It was a world of cramped quarters, of engine noise so constant it became a form of silence, of sleep snatched in thirty-minute intervals between watches. Bob Sr. graduated from the scow to an aircraft carrier, where the stakes grew higher and the responsibilities heavier. As a master electrician, he held lives in his hands every time he traced a circuit or repaired a generator. One mistake in a ship's electrical system could mean not just darkness but death—planes unable to launch, pumps unable to fight fires, communications severed at the moment of maximum danger.
    84|
    85|Psychologists who study military service often note its lasting impact on personality traits. High-stress environments, particularly those involving genuine mortal danger, tend to increase conscientiousness and attention to detail. They can also, in some cases, create patterns of hypervigilance and emotional regulation that prove difficult to shed when the uniform comes off.  Bob Sr. returned from the Pacific War changed. He had seen things, survived things, shouldered responsibilities that no teenager should have to bear. He married Bob's mother in a clandestine elopement—their families would not bless the union because she was Catholic and he was Protestant, and the religious hatred between their households ran deep enough to cut. After World War II, they moved into his parents' partially finished, unheated summer cottage, two young people trying to build a life in a structure meant for vacation weekends. Then came the recall.
    86|
    87|When North Korean forces poured across the 38th parallel in 1950, Bob Sr.'s decision to stay in the Naval Reserves—made for sensible economic reasons in peacetime—became a doorway back into war. He served on an aircraft carrier in the Korean conflict, returning to Michigan only after the armistice of 1953. By then, his wife was pregnant with their first child, a boy they would name Robert, after the generations of Roberts before him. The GI Bill made possible what would otherwise have been impossible: a small home purchased with a low-cost mortgage, a foothold in the American middle class for a working-class sailor with an elementary school education. In the fall of 1952, Bob was born. A baby brother followed. The family was complete, or so it seemed.
    88|
    89|### The Household Regiment
    90|
    91|Bob's earliest coherent memories of his father are of a man who seemed to exist in a state of perpetual vigilance, as if still standing watch on a carrier deck. Saturdays in the Mills household were not days of rest. They were days of chores, of inspections, of tasks assigned with military precision and expected to be completed to military standards. Bob Sr. treated his sons not as children but as sailors—raw recruits who needed to be broken down and rebuilt into capable men. This was authoritative parenting, psychological researchers would later classify it: high expectations coupled with (in theory) strong emotional support. But for young Bob, the firstborn, the emotional support often felt lost in translation, drowned out by the volume of his father's voice. That voice. It wasn't that Bob Sr. was angry, not really. Those who understand military training recognize the difference between rage and command presence. Bob Sr. had learned to project authority across engine rooms and flight decks, to make himself heard over the scream of jets and the roar of machinery. When he brought that voice home, he thought he was preparing his sons for a world he knew to be unforgiving. What he didn't understand was that a child is not a sailor, and a living room is not a ship.
    92|
    93|Bob's younger brother resisted passively. He would rock nervously. But Bob took a different path. He learned to comply, to anticipate, to internalize the expectations until they became his own. He cleaned his room. He completed his chores without complaint. He tried , in essence, the model sailor his father wanted never quite meeting the adult standards.
    94|
    95|There was tenderness in Bob Sr., too, though it expressed itself obliquely. The man was a craftsman of extraordinary versatility—electrician by trade, but also plumber, carpenter, model builder. He found his peace in the garage, surrounded by the scent of sawdust and glue, constructing U-control and radio-controlled aircraft from balsa wood and tissue paper. These weren't toys; they were engineering challenges, miniature aircraft that demanded the same precision as their full-sized counterparts. The garage became Bob's summer classroom. Under his father's tutelage, he learned to read blueprints, to calculate weight distributions, to understand the aerodynamic principles that kept fragile structures aloft. Other neighborhood boys joined them, drawn by the spectacle of flight and the charisma of a man who could make the impossible seem achievable. Bob Sr. never turned a boy away. The garage became a sanctuary not just for him but for a whole generation of neighborhood young people seeking the approval of a father figure who demanded excellence and offered, in return, the satisfaction of creation.  Years later, Bob would recognize this pattern: his father's harshness and his generosity, his demanding nature and his dedication, all facets of a man trying to love his sons in the only language he had been taught. By the time Bob's third brother arrived, years after Bob himself, Bob Sr. had softened considerably. Experience had taught him that children weren't sailors, that love didn't require drill sergeant volume to be effective. But for Bob, the firstborn, the die had already been cast.
    96|
    97|### The Plate
    98|
    99|If the garage represented Bob Sr. at his best, the dinner table represented something more complicated. Bobs father was overweight—not grotesquely so, not in a way that would have attracted comment in 1950s America, where physical labor was still common and body standards were less exacting than they would become. But they carried the weight of their generation, the legacy of Depression-era scarcity and wartime rationing that had programmed their bodies to treat every meal as potentially the last. They also carried the beliefs of their era about parenting. Providing food was love. Making children eat that food was responsibility. And ensuring that nothing was wasted—*clean your plate*—was moral duty inherited from ancestors who had known genuine hunger.  The problem was that Bob Sr. had no conception of child-sized portions. When he served dinner, he heaped his sons' plates with adult quantities of meat and potatoes and vegetables. And when he said "clean your plate," he meant it literally. His sons would not leave the table until every scrap was consumed.

   602|### InnoCentive
   603|
   604|InnoCentive was unlike anything Bob had ever encountered — a marketplace for ideas where anyone with a problem could post it and anyone with a solution could solve it.    607|
   608|### The Partnership Mature
   609|
   610|Cindy changed Bob. Not in the ways Nancy changed him — those changes were formative, foundational, the construction of the person Bob became during adulthood. Cindy's changes were different. Refinements. Adjustments. The sanding of rough edges Bob did not know he possessed.
   611|

   619|
   620|Bob spends more time with machines than he once did. The 3D printer humming beside his desk. The AI systems he queries and tests and occasionally argues with.    624|## Chapter 11: What Remains Unwritten

   626|### The Daughter's Story
   627|
   628|There is nothing that terrifies a parent more than a sick child.    649|
   650|Life is harder than you expect and more beautiful than you imagine. The difficulties will test you. The beauty will sustain you. Neither optimism nor pessimism serves well as a compass.    652|Love is not a feeling but a practice. It requires attention, maintenance, the daily choice to show up for the people you have committed to. The feeling comes and goes. The practice stays.    653|
   654|Failure is not the opposite of success but its prerequisite. You will fail. Repeatedly. The question is not whether you fail but what you learn, whether you have the resilience to try again.    656|Technology is a tool, not a solution. It can amplify human capability for good or ill. The direction depends on human choices, human values, human wisdom. Do not surrender your agency to the machines. Maintain your judgment. Use the tools; do not let them use you.

   660|Time is the only genuine currency. How you spend your hours is how you spend your life. Guard them jealously. Give them generously to what matters.    668|### Facing Mortality

   675|

   684|## Chapter 12: The Threshold
